title: HTTP and Request Security knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of “HTTP and Request Security”?
options: HTTP and Request Security means the browser can enforce all permissions without the backend.
HTTP and Request Security removes the need for error handling, accessibility checks and tests.
HTTP and Request Security should be implemented by copying a snippet without checking the Angular version.
HTTP and Request Security helps explain and implement one part of an Angular application; choose the API pattern that matches the behavior and verify it.
questions.answer_key: HTTP and Request Security helps explain and implement one part of an Angular application; choose the API pattern that matches the behavior and verify it.
questions.explanation: HTTP and Request Security is a concept in the supplied Angular curriculum. Its correct application depends on the intended behavior, surrounding context and verification.

questions.prompt: How should a learner work with “HTTPS” in this lesson?
options: Assume “HTTPS” works identically across every Angular major and runtime.
Use “HTTPS” to bypass runtime validation of external or user-provided values.
Connect “HTTPS” to the lesson goal, use a focused example, and validate the behavior in the selected Angular environment.
Treat “HTTPS” as a reason to skip the surrounding application context.
questions.answer_key: Connect “HTTPS” to the lesson goal, use a focused example, and validate the behavior in the selected Angular environment.
questions.explanation: The PDF explicitly lists “HTTPS” under HTTP and Request Security. Anchor it in a small example and check the behavior rather than relying on a memorized phrase.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest verification approach for “HTTP and Request Security”?
options: Ignore a failing test if the component looks correct in one browser.
Run the example in a compatible local Angular workspace, test the expected result and one failure case, and document any version limitation.
Assume an SVG diagram proves the code compiled and passed tests.
Treat a successful client-side render as backend authorization evidence.
questions.answer_key: Run the example in a compatible local Angular workspace, test the expected result and one failure case, and document any version limitation.
questions.explanation: Verification evidence should match the running environment. Static teaching snippets are not compiler output, and frontend checks do not replace backend authorization.
